what-is-avd.title: What AVD is — inputs → structured config → CLI
what-is-avd.summary: Follow one line of dc1-leaf1a's config back through the structured config to the group_vars that produced it.

blocks.text:
Arista Validated Designs (AVD) turns a **description of your fabric** into **device configurations**. You never write
`router bgp 65101` by hand — you write *"the leafs dc1-leaf1a and dc1-leaf1b are an l3leaf pair in AS 65101"* and AVD
works out the rest. In AVD 6.4 this is a pipeline of two stages, which avdlab runs for you with **pyavd** when you press
**Build**:

1. **`eos_designs`** reads the *AVD Design* inputs — your `group_vars/*.yml` (fabric name, node types, pools, tenants,
   endpoints) — validates them against the schema and computes a **structured configuration** per device:
   `intended/structured_configs/dc1-leaf1a.yml`. This is the *EOS Config* data model, a YAML mirror of the CLI.
2. **`eos_cli_config_gen`** turns each structured config 1:1 into CLI text — `intended/configs/dc1-leaf1a.cfg` — and a
   Markdown document — `documentation/devices/dc1-leaf1a.md`.

Everything happens **offline**: no switch is needed to build. Deploying (containerlab startup-config, eAPI config
replace, or CloudVision) and validating (ANTA) are separate steps.

Take a concrete line. In the default lab, `dc1-leaf1a` has:

```
interface Loopback0
   description ROUTER_ID
   ip address 10.255.0.3/32
```

In the structured config the same thing is `loopback_interfaces: [{name: Loopback0, description: ROUTER_ID,
ip_address: 10.255.0.3/32}]`. And in the inputs? Nowhere does `10.255.0.3` appear! `group_vars/DC1_L3_LEAVES.yml`
only says `loopback_ipv4_pool: 10.255.0.0/27`, `loopback_ipv4_offset: 2` and `id: 1` for dc1-leaf1a. AVD computed
10.255.0.0/27 → address #(1 + 2) = 10.255.0.3. That is the whole idea: **you describe intent and numbering rules,
AVD derives the values** — consistently on both ends of every link.

blocks.label: Open dc1-leaf1a's CLI and click "interface Loopback0" to explain it

blocks.text:
Because eos_cli_config_gen reads **only** the structured config files, EOS Config keys you put directly into
group_vars (for example a top-level `ethernet_interfaces:`) are **ignored** after eos_designs has run — AVD 6 warns
about it. The supported ways to add raw configuration are covered in the lesson on escape hatches.

blocks.label: The build produced a structured config for dc1-leaf1a
blocks.hint: Run a build first (Build tab → Build).

blocks.label: dc1-leaf1a's CLI contains Loopback0 10.255.0.3/32
blocks.hint: With default pools the address is 10.255.0.3; if you changed the loopback pool, adapt the expectation.

blocks.question: You add `ethernet_interfaces:` with a description for Ethernet10 directly to group_vars/FABRIC.yml and build. What happens?
options: The description appears on Ethernet10 of every device
Nothing — eos_cli_config_gen reads the structured config files, so top-level EOS Config keys in the design inputs are ignored (AVD warns)
The build fails with a schema error
blocks.explanation: Since AVD 6.0 eos_cli_config_gen renders from intended/structured_configs only. Use custom_structured_configuration_ethernet_interfaces or a node structured_config instead.

blocks.text:
**Takeaway:** AVD is a compiler — *design inputs* (`group_vars`) → `eos_designs` → *structured config* →
`eos_cli_config_gen` → *CLI + docs*. Read a config line backwards through that chain and you will always find the
input (and the numbering rule) that produced it.

pools-ip-math.title: Pools and the IP math (loopbacks, P2P, MLAG)
pools-ip-math.summary: Derive every address of dc1-leaf1b by hand from four pools and its id.

blocks.text:
AVD never asks you for a per-interface address in an L3LS fabric. It asks for **pools** and computes addresses with one
helper: take the pool, cut it into subnets of a prefix length, pick subnet number *N*, then host *M*. A pool is a
comma-separated list of prefixes or ranges (`10.255.0.0/27, 10.9.9.10-10.9.9.20`).

The default lab's pools (knob **IP pools**, written to `l3leaf.defaults` / `spine.defaults`):

| pool | value | used for |
|---|---|---|
| `loopback_ipv4_pool` | 10.255.0.0/27 | Loopback0 = router-id, EVPN peering |
| `vtep_loopback_ipv4_pool` | 10.255.1.0/27 | Loopback1 = VXLAN source |
| `uplink_ipv4_pool` | 10.255.255.0/26 | /31 P2P links leaf ↔ spine |
| `mlag_peer_ipv4_pool` | 10.255.1.64/27 | Vlan4094 (MLAG control) |
| `mlag_peer_l3_ipv4_pool` | 10.255.1.96/27 | Vlan4093 + per-VRF peering SVIs |

Now do **dc1-leaf1b** (id 2, MLAG secondary of DC1_L3_LEAF1, `loopback_ipv4_offset: 2`):

- **Loopback0** = /32 #(id + offset) = #(2 + 2) → **10.255.0.4**. The spines took #1 and #2 of the same pool.
- **Loopback1 (VTEP)** — MLAG pairs share one VTEP, computed from the **primary's** id: #(1 + 2) → **10.255.1.3** on
  both dc1-leaf1a and dc1-leaf1b.
- **Uplinks** — /31 number = (id − 1) × `max_uplink_switches` × `max_parallel_uplinks` + uplink index.
  With 2 spines: (2 − 1) × 2 × 1 + 0 = **#2** → 10.255.255.4/31 → leaf **.5**, spine1 **.4**; second uplink #3 →
  leaf **.7**, spine2 **.6**. The child (leaf) takes +1, the parent (spine) +0.
- **MLAG** (`fabric_ip_addressing.mlag.algorithm: first_id`) — /31 number = primary id − 1 = 0; primary +0, secondary +1:
  Vlan4094 **10.255.1.65**, Vlan4093 **10.255.1.97**; the peer is .64 / .96.

The same pools also build `ip prefix-list PL-LOOPBACKS-EVPN-OVERLAY` (`permit 10.255.0.0/27 eq 32`, `permit
10.255.1.0/27 eq 32`), which filters what is redistributed into the underlay. If a loopback is outside those pools it
is never advertised and the overlay stays down.

Try it — move the loopback pool to 10.254.0.0/27 (then rebuild and watch every Loopback0 change)
dc1-leaf1b Loopback0 matches loopback_ipv4_pool #(id + offset)

blocks.question: You add a third spine (uplink_switches gets 3 entries, max_uplink_switches follows). What happens to dc1-leaf1b's first uplink address?
options: It stays 10.255.255.5 — existing links never move
It changes — the /31 number becomes (2 − 1) × 3 + 0 = #3, so every leaf's links are renumbered

blocks.explanation: max_uplink_switches is part of the formula. Set max_uplink_switches higher from day one to reserve space if you expect to add spines.

blocks.question: Why does the l3leaf group set loopback_ipv4_offset: 2?
options: Because the spines use ids 1 and 2 in the same loopback pool
Because Loopback0 must be an even address
blocks.explanation: Spines and leafs share 10.255.0.0/27. Without the offset dc1-leaf1a (id 1) would get 10.255.0.1 — dc1-spine1's router-id.

anta-validation.title: ANTA: how validation works and reading a report
anta-validation.summary: AVD writes per-device ANTA catalogs from the structured configs; ANTA runs them over eAPI and reports success / failure / error / skipped.

blocks.text:
Building tells you what the network **should** be; **ANTA** (Arista Network Test Automation, 1.10 in this lab) checks
what it **is**. AVD bridges the two: during the build it generates a **catalog per device** from the structured config —
`anta/avd_catalogs/dc1-leaf1a.json` — containing only tests that make sense for that device, with expected values
filled in: `VerifyBGPPeerSession` with dc1-leaf1a's real peers (10.255.255.0, 10.255.255.2, 10.255.0.1 …),
`VerifyLLDPNeighbors` with the expected neighbor on every link (Ethernet1 → dc1-spine1 Ethernet1),
`VerifyMlagStatus`, `VerifyVxlanConfigSanity`, `VerifyRoutingProtocolModel` (multi-agent), `VerifyInterfacesStatus`,
`VerifyReachability` over each P2P /31 …

**Validate** (Validation tab) runs ANTA against the deployed lab over eAPI (the `arista` user, HTTPS on the management
IPs). Each test yields one of:

| status | meaning |
|---|---|
| **success** | the device matches the intent |
| **failure** | the test ran and the state is wrong (BGP peer not Established, LLDP neighbor missing …) |
| **error** | the test could not run (command failed, timeout, unreachable device) |
| **skipped** | not applicable (e.g. hardware tests on cEOSLab — AVD does not even generate them for virtual platforms) |

The lab skips `VerifyNTP` and `VerifyReloadCause` by default (`avd_catalogs_filters` — containers rarely have a usable
NTP source or a clean reload cause) and enables `avd_catalogs_extra_fabric_validation` (fabric-wide reachability, e.g.
VTEP to VTEP). Reports are JSON / Markdown / CSV per run.

How to read a failing report: sort by **device**, then by **category**. A failing `VerifyLLDPNeighbors` usually means a
cabling (topology) mistake; `VerifyBGPPeerSession` failing on the overlay but not the underlay points at loopback
reachability (`PL-LOOPBACKS-EVPN-OVERLAY`, pools); MLAG failures at the peer-link or node_group; errors on one device
at its reachability or credentials.

Open the Validation tab to read the report
The last validation job succeeded

blocks.label: The last report has no failures or errors

blocks.question: dc1-leaf2b was powered off during the run. Which status do its tests most likely show?
options: error — the tests could not collect any output
blocks.explanation: failure means the test ran and found a wrong state; an unreachable device cannot run its commands, which ANTA reports as error.

blocks.question: Where do the expected values in the AVD-generated catalogs come from?
options: From the structured configs of the build (intent), not from raw_eos_cli or the device
blocks.explanation: AVD builds catalogs from intended/structured_configs — which is why raw_eos_cli additions are invisible to them.

blocks.text:
**Takeaway:** build = intent, ANTA = reality. AVD turns the intent into per-device catalogs; validation compares; read
reports by device and category, and map failures back to the input that should have produced the missing state.

glossary.short: Arista Network Test Automation — runs test catalogs against devices over eAPI and reports success / failure / error / skipped.
A list of ANTA tests with inputs. AVD generates one per device from its structured config (anta/avd_catalogs/<host>.json), tagged with the hostname.
The same gateway IP and MAC on every leaf (ip_address_virtual → `ip address virtual 10.10.11.1/24` + virtual_router_mac_address), so hosts can move freely.
Arista Validated Designs — an Ansible collection and Python library (pyavd) that turns a fabric description into EOS configs, docs and tests.
glossary.long: AVD's pipeline is eos_designs (design inputs → structured config) and eos_cli_config_gen (structured config → CLI + docs). avdlab runs it with pyavd 6.4.

glossary.short: The eos_designs input model — fabric_name, node types, pools, tenants, connected endpoints … usually in group_vars.
Containerised EOS for labs. AVD platform cEOSLab — Management1, no hardware tests, BGP wait-install flags off.
Arista's management plane (CVaaS in the cloud or on-prem) — telemetry via TerminAttr, config via Static Configuration Studio, change controls.
Devices plugged into the fabric (servers, firewalls, routers …) described by name and adapters (switches, switch_ports, VLANs, port_channel) — AVD configures the switch ports.
Tool that runs network labs as containers (cEOS-lab + linux clients) wired with veth pairs; avdlab builds its topology from AVD's topology CSV.
Escape hatch — variables named custom_structured_configuration_<eos key> are merged onto the generated structured config last.
glossary.long: List items with a primary key are merged by key (custom_structured_configuration_list_merge, default append_rp). Prefer a design-model key when one exists; raw_eos_cli is the last resort.

glossary.short: AVD role that pushes intended configs and tags to CloudVision through a workspace and a change control; devices are matched by serial number first.
Per type/platform default uplink, MLAG and downlink ports (e.g. l3leaf uplinks Ethernet1-2, MLAG Ethernet3-4; spine downlinks Ethernet1-8). AVD ships none — the fabric defines them.
EOS JSON-RPC API over HTTPS (management api http-commands) used by Ansible deploys and ANTA. Enabled with management_eapi.enabled (off by default since AVD 6.0).
External BGP — sessions between different AS numbers. In the lab spines are AS 65100 and each leaf pair its own AS (65101, 65102).
The AVD role/stage that turns a structured config 1:1 into EOS CLI (intended/configs) and device Markdown docs.
The AVD role/stage that reads the design data model (group_vars) and produces one structured config per device.
glossary.long: It validates the inputs against the schema, computes fabric-wide facts (peers, pools, route servers) and renders the EOS Config model. It never talks to devices.

glossary.short: Ethernet Segment Identifier — EVPN all-active multihoming across switches that are not an MLAG pair (adapter ethernet_segment.short_esi).
Ethernet VPN (BGP address family l2vpn evpn) — the control plane that distributes MAC/IP bindings, flood lists and IP prefixes between VTEPs.
Type-1 Ethernet A-D (multihoming), type-2 MAC/IP advertisement, type-3 inclusive multicast (flood list / VTEP discovery), type-4 Ethernet segment (DF election), type-5 IP prefix.
Required. The inventory group that contains every device of the fabric (FABRIC); peer facts are computed across it.
Ansible variables per inventory group (group_vars/<GROUP>.yml). A device sees the merged vars of all its groups; child groups override parents.
Internal BGP — sessions inside one AS, e.g. between the two MLAG peers (MLAG-IPv4-UNDERLAY-PEER, AS 65101) or an iBGP overlay with route reflectors.
inventory.yml — the tree of groups (FABRIC → DC1 → DC1_SPINES / DC1_L3_LEAVES / DC1_L2_LEAVES) and hosts with their ansible_host (management IP).
The VNI of a VLAN (bridging) — mac_vrf_vni_base + VLAN id, e.g. VLAN 11 → 10011.
The VNI of a VRF (routing between VTEPs, symmetric IRB, type-5 routes) — vrf_vni, e.g. VRF10 → 10.
Added to the node id when picking a loopback from a pool shared by several node types (the l3leafs use the spine count, 2, so dc1-leaf1a gets 10.255.0.3).
Number of uplink slots reserved per node in the P2P formula (default = number of uplink_switches). Changing it renumbers every uplink — set it high early if spines may be added.
Multi-chassis LAG — two switches present one LACP partner to a device. AVD forms it for two-node node_groups; peer-link Port-Channel3, Vlan4094/4093, domain-id = group name.
A group of nodes of one type sharing settings (e.g. DC1_L3_LEAF1 with bgp_as 65101). Exactly two nodes of an MLAG-capable type form an MLAG pair; the group name becomes the MLAG domain-id.
The node's number — the index into every pool (loopbacks, VTEP, uplink /31s, MLAG) and into the parent's downlink interfaces.
The table of node behaviours (spine, l3leaf, l2leaf, l3spine, leaf, p, pe, rr, wan_router …) — underlay router, VTEP, MLAG support, services. A device picks one with `type`.
glossary.long: Settings for a type live under its key (spine:, l3leaf:, l2leaf:) as defaults → node_groups → nodes (most specific wins). custom_node_type_keys adds or replaces entries. design.type was removed in AVD 6.0.

glossary.short: The virtual network on top of the underlay — here EVPN over BGP sessions between Loopback0s, carrying MAC/IP and prefix routes for VXLAN.
A routed fabric link leaf ↔ spine with a /31 from uplink_ipv4_pool; the child (leaf) takes +1, the parent (spine) +0.
The link between the two MLAG peers (Port-Channel from mlag_interfaces, trunk group MLAG) carrying the peer VLANs and failover traffic.
A comma-separated list of prefixes/ranges AVD carves addresses from by node id (loopback_ipv4_pool, vtep_loopback_ipv4_pool, uplink_ipv4_pool, mlag_peer_ipv4_pool …).
glossary.long: Loopback0 = pool[id + loopback_ipv4_offset]; P2P /31 number = (id − 1) × max_uplink_switches × max_parallel_uplinks + uplink index; MLAG /31 = primary id − 1 (algorithm first_id).

glossary.short: A reusable set of adapter settings (mode, VLANs, portfast …) referenced by `profile:`; precedence adapter > profile > parent_profile.
The Python package behind AVD (validate_inputs, get_avd_facts, get_device_structured_config, get_device_config) — used by avdlab instead of Ansible to build labs.
Verbatim EOS CLI appended at a scope (node, VRF, SVI, interface, platform). Not validated, not documented, invisible to generated ANTA catalogs.
Makes each VTEP's routes unique in BGP — AVD default <Loopback0>:<number>, e.g. 10.255.0.3:10011 for VLAN 11 on dc1-leaf1a.
The iBGP equivalent of a route server — reflects routes between iBGP clients (route-reflector-client). Used with iBGP overlays and MPLS designs (rr nodes).
An EVPN peer that relays routes between clients without changing the next hop (spines, evpn_role server, next-hop-unchanged). Clients use their uplink_switches as evpn_route_servers.
Extended community deciding which VTEPs import a route — identical fabric-wide, e.g. 10011:10011 for VLAN 11, 10:10 for VRF10.
EOS policy inside a VRF — segments (prefixes) and per-application policies attached to the destination segment; the lab's Segmentation knob renders it on the L3 leafs.
The per-device YAML in the EOS Config data model (intended/structured_configs/<host>.yml) — the output of eos_designs and the only input of eos_cli_config_gen.
Switched Virtual Interface — the routed interface of a VLAN (interface Vlan11). Must set enabled true or AVD renders it shut down.
The top of the network services model — a tenant has mac_vrf_vni_base, VRFs (with SVIs) and L2 VLANs.
The EOS streaming agent that sends state to CloudVision; rendered as `daemon TerminAttr` from cv_settings.
The routed network between switches that makes every loopback/VTEP reachable — here eBGP over the P2P /31s, advertising only loopbacks.
Virtual ARP — a shared virtual IP/MAC on top of unique per-switch SVI addresses (ip_virtual_router_addresses). ip address virtual (anycast) needs no per-switch IPs.
VXLAN Network Identifier (24 bits). L2VNI per VLAN, L3VNI per VRF.
A separate routing table. Tenant VRFs (VRF10, VRF11) carry the SVIs; MGMT is the out-of-band management VRF.
VXLAN Tunnel End Point — the switch that encapsulates/decapsulates VXLAN, sourced from Loopback1 (vtep_loopback_ipv4_pool). An MLAG pair shares one VTEP IP.
Virtual eXtensible LAN — encapsulates Ethernet frames in UDP (port 4789) between VTEPs; a 24-bit VNI identifies the segment.
EOS day-0 boot without config — DHCP gives an address and option 67 bootfile; a `#!` script is executed, anything else becomes the startup-config.

steps.title: Create a lab
steps.text: Start from a template — single-dc-l3ls is the classic EVPN/VXLAN fabric (2 spines, 2 MLAG leaf pairs, 2 L2 leafs).

steps.title: Pick a template
steps.text: Each template is an AVD example turned into a form. The tags tell you what it teaches (l3ls, evpn, mlag …).

steps.title: Knobs
steps.text: Knobs write AVD inputs (group_vars) for you. Hover (i) on any knob to see which AVD keys it writes and what CLI it renders.

steps.title: Build
steps.text: Build runs eos_designs + eos_cli_config_gen (pyavd) offline — no switch needed. It writes structured configs, CLI, documentation and ANTA catalogs.

steps.title: Read the result
steps.text: In Files, click any line of intended/configs/<host>.cfg to see which input produced it.

steps.title: Deploy
steps.text: Deploy starts the containers on your lab host with the intended configs as startup-config.

steps.title: Validate
steps.text: Validate runs the AVD-generated ANTA catalogs against the live switches.

steps.title: Add a host
steps.text: A lab host is a Linux machine (VM or bare metal) reachable over SSH that runs Docker + containerlab.

steps.title: SSH key
steps.text: Generate a key and paste the public key into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the host — the private key stays encrypted in avdlab.

steps.title: Probe
steps.text: Probe collects CPU, memory, Docker/containerlab versions and kernel settings and tells you what to fix (e.g. inotify limits for many cEOS).

steps.title: Bootstrap
steps.text: Bootstrap installs Docker, containerlab and the sysctls idempotently; every step reports skip / apply / ok.

steps.title: Capabilities
steps.text: The capability panel shows what the host can run and which cEOS images are already present.

steps.title: The fabric graph
steps.text: Nodes and links come from AVD's topology CSV — every link AVD knows about is a veth pair in containerlab.

steps.title: Edit mode
steps.text: Edits are stored as overrides on top of the knobs (uplink_switches, uplink_switch_interfaces, endpoints), so AVD stays the source of truth.

steps.title: Add an endpoint
steps.text: Adding a server writes a connected endpoint (servers[].adapters) — rebuild and the switch ports are configured for you.

steps.title: Hot-add a test host
steps.text: On a deployed lab you can plug a client into a free port without redeploying the fabric.

steps.title: Inspect
steps.text: Click a node or link to see its management IP, role, interfaces and quick actions.

steps.title: Run ANTA
steps.text: Runs the per-device catalogs AVD generated from the structured configs (NTP and reload-cause tests are skipped by default on containers).

steps.title: Totals
steps.text: success = matches intent, failure = wrong state, error = test could not run, skipped = not applicable.

steps.title: Read by device, then category
steps.text: LLDP failures usually mean cabling, BGP overlay failures loopback reachability, MLAG failures the peer-link or node_group.

steps.title: Reports
steps.text: Every run keeps JSON, Markdown and CSV reports in the lab's git history.

steps.title: Targets
steps.text: Add a CVaaS tenant or an on-prem cluster with a service-account token (stored encrypted).

steps.title: Streaming
steps.text: The lab's CloudVision knob renders cv_settings → daemon TerminAttr (needs NTP, and DNS for CVaaS).

steps.title: Onboard
steps.text: Onboarding writes the token to each switch (never into the config) so TerminAttr can register.

steps.title: cv_deploy
steps.text: Pushes the intended configs as configlets through a workspace and a change control, matching devices by serial number.

eos_designs:tenants.vrfs.description:
VRFs will only be configured on a node if any of the underlying objects like `svis`, `l3_interfaces` or `l3_port_channels` apply to the node.

It is recommended to only define a VRF in one Tenant. If the same VRF name is used across multiple tenants and those tenants
are accepted by `filter.tenants` on the node, any object set under the duplicate VRFs must either be unique or be an exact match.

VRF "default" is partially supported under network-services. Currently the supported options for "default" vrf are route-target,
route-distinguisher settings, structured_config, raw_eos_cli in bgp and SVIs are the only supported interface type.
Vlan-aware-bundles are supported as well inside default vrf. OSPF is not supported currently.

eos_designs:tenants.vrfs.vrf_vni.description:
Required if "vrf_id" is not set.
The VRF VNI range is not limited, but if vrf_id is not set, "vrf_vni" is used for calculating MLAG iBGP peering vlan id.
"vrf_vni" may also be used for VRF RD/RT ID. See "overlay_rd_type" and "overlay_rt_type" for details.
See "mlag_ibgp_peering_vrfs.base_vlan" for details.
If vrf_vni > 10000 make sure to adjust "mac_vrf_vni_base" accordingly to avoid overlap.

eos_designs:tenants.mac_vrf_vni_base.description:
Base number for MAC VRF VXLAN Network Identifier (required with VXLAN).
VXLAN VNI is derived from the base number with simple addition.
i.e. mac_vrf_vni_base = 10000, svi 100 = VNI 10100, svi 300 = VNI 10300.

dc_name.summary: Name of the data centre. It prefixes every hostname (dc1-spine1, dc1-leaf1a …) and, upper-cased, the inventory groups (DC1, DC1_SPINES, DC1_L3_LEAVES …).

mgmt_subnet.summary: Out-of-band management subnet. The l3ls generator numbers `mgmt_ip` from it — spines .11+, L3 leafs .101+, L2 leafs .151+ — and uses it as the containerlab management network.
mgmt_subnet.renders: interface Management1 / vrf MGMT / ip address 172.16.1.101/24
pitfalls: Must not overlap the host's own networks or another lab's management network on the same host.
The gateway (mgmt_gateway) must be inside this subnet.

mgmt_gateway.summary: Default gateway of the management VRF. AVD renders a static default route in VRF MGMT towards it.
pitfalls: Must be an address inside mgmt_subnet; on containerlab it is the management bridge's gateway.
A node-level `mgmt_gateway` overrides the global one.

ceos_version.renders: Nothing in the EOS config; `image: arista/ceos:4.34.2F` in clab/topology.clab.yml
pitfalls: The image must exist on the lab host (Images page → download / push).
Very old EOS versions may reject CLI that AVD 6.4 renders (AVD targets current EOS syntax, EOS 4.35 ordering).

ceos_arch.summary: CPU architecture of the cEOS image — x86_64 (arista/ceos:<version>) or arm64 (arista/ceos:<version>-arm64, cEOSarm). Must match the lab host.
ceos_arch.renders: Nothing in the EOS config; selects the image tag in the containerlab topology
pitfalls: An x86_64 image on an ARM host (or vice versa) will not boot.

device_password.summary: Password of the `arista` admin user on every switch (hashed to sha512) and of the BGP peer groups (type-7, encrypted per peer-group name). Ansible and ANTA log in with it.
device_password.renders: username arista privilege 15 role network-admin secret sha512 $6$…; neighbor EVPN-OVERLAY-PEERS password 7 …
pitfalls: The type-7 BGP password is keyed on the peer-group NAME — renaming a peer group invalidates a pre-encrypted password (use cleartext_password instead).
Changing it on a deployed lab requires a deploy; until then Ansible/ANTA use the new password against the old config and fail to log in.

spine_count.summary: Number of spines. Every L3 leaf gets one uplink per spine (uplink_switches), each spine is an EVPN route server for all leafs.
spine_count.renders: interface Ethernet1..N (P2P_dc1-spineN_…) on each leaf; one EVPN neighbor per spine; spine Loopback0 = pool #1..N
pitfalls: loopback_ipv4_offset of the leafs follows the spine count (spines use Loopback0
The P2P /31 formula uses max_uplink_switches = number of spines, so adding a spine renumbers every uplink.
With more than 2 spines the leaf uplinks become Ethernet1-4 and the MLAG peer-link moves to Ethernet5-6.

leaf_pairs.summary: Number of L3 leaf MLAG pairs. Each pair is one node_group with two nodes (MLAG is automatic) and its own BGP AS; leaf ids run 1..2N.
leaf_pairs.renders: mlag configuration / domain-id DC1_L3_LEAF<n>; router bgp <leaf_asn_base+n-1>; one P2P link per spine per leaf
pitfalls: Node ids index every pool — the loopback, VTEP and uplink pools must be large enough (a /27 loopback pool holds ids up to 31 minus the offset).
Spine downlinks (default_interfaces) are extended automatically past Ethernet8 for more than 4 pairs.

l2leaf_per_pair.summary: L2 leafs under each L3 leaf pair — 0 (none), 1 (dc1-leaf<n>c) or 2 (an MLAG pair c/d). L2 leafs are `l2leaf` nodes with port-channel uplinks to the pair.
l2leaf_per_pair.renders: interface Port-Channel1 (L2_DC1_L3_LEAF1_Port-Channel8) on the L2 leaf; interface Port-Channel8 … mlag 8 on the L3 leafs
pitfalls: L2 leafs are not underlay routers (no ip routing, no BGP); their trunk VLANs are computed from the VLANs they render.
With 2 per pair the L2 leafs form their own MLAG pair (Ethernet3-4 peer-link) and need their own mlag_peer_ipv4_pool.

pools.summary: The IP pools AVD carves addresses from by node id — loopback (Loopback0 / router-id), vtep (Loopback1), uplink (/31 P2P links), mlag_peer (Vlan4094) and mlag_l3 (Vlan4093 + per-VRF peering SVIs).
pools.renders: interface Loopback0 / ip address 10.255.0.3/32; interface Loopback1 / ip address 10.255.1.3/32; interface Ethernet1 / ip address 10.255.255.1/31; interface Vlan4094 / ip address 10.255.1.64/31; ip prefix-list PL-LOOPBACKS-EVPN-OVERLAY
pitfalls: Loopback0 = pool[id + loopback_ipv4_offset]; spines and leafs share the loopback pool, so the leaf offset (= spine count) keeps them apart.
MLAG pairs share ONE VTEP address (pool[primary id + offset]).
P2P subnet offset = (id - 1) × max_uplink_switches × max_parallel_uplinks + uplink index — size the uplink pool for the largest id.
Pools also feed PL-LOOPBACKS-EVPN-OVERLAY — a pool that does not cover the loopbacks stops them from being advertised and the overlay never comes up.

spine_asn.summary: BGP AS shared by all spines (eBGP underlay and overlay; the spines are EVPN route servers).
spine_asn.renders: router bgp 65100 on the spines; neighbor … remote-as 65100 on every leaf
pitfalls: Spines in one AS never peer with each other, and a route from one leaf is not reflected back to a leaf in the same AS — which is why every leaf pair has its own AS.

leaf_asn_base.summary: BGP AS of the first L3 leaf pair; pair n gets leaf_asn_base + n - 1. Both MLAG peers of a pair share the AS (set on the node_group).
leaf_asn_base.renders: router bgp 65101 on dc1-leaf1a/b, 65102 on dc1-leaf2a/b; neighbor MLAG-IPv4-UNDERLAY-PEER remote-as 65101
pitfalls: MLAG peers must share their AS — put bgp_as on the node_group, not on the nodes.
Use 4-byte private ASNs (4200000000+) for large fabrics; quote asdot values ("65000.100") in YAML.

serial_scheme.summary: Python format string for every node's serial number (PREFIX = first 4 characters of the lab slug, ID = position in the inventory; HOST, TYPE, SLUG also available). Written to `serial_number` and to the cEOS ceos-config file, so the container boots with that serial.
serial_scheme.renders: Nothing in the CLI; metadata.serial_number in the structured config, documentation and `SERIALNUMBER=` in clab/<node>/ceos-config
pitfalls: CloudVision and cv_deploy identify devices by serial number first — keep serials unique across labs that stream to the same CloudVision tenant.
Changing the scheme on an onboarded lab makes CloudVision see new devices.

tenants.summary: The network services — tenants with VRFs (L3VNI), SVIs (anycast gateways, L2VNI) and L2 VLANs, edited as the AVD `tenants:` YAML list and validated with pyavd.
tenants.renders: vlan 11 / name VRF10_VLAN11; vrf instance VRF10; interface Vlan11 / ip address virtual 10.10.11.1/24; vxlan vlan 11 vni 10011; vxlan vrf VRF10 vni 10; router bgp … vlan 11 / rd 10.255.0.3:10011; vrf VRF10 / rd 10.255.0.3:10
pitfalls: L2VNI = mac_vrf_vni_base + VLAN id; RD/RT use the same number — keep it within 16 bits when the RD admin field is an IP.
`ip_address_virtual` needs `virtual_router_mac_address` on the leafs (set by the generator).
A VRF is only rendered on nodes where at least one of its SVIs matches the node's filter (tenants/tags).

servers.summary: Connected endpoints (`servers:` list) — which switch ports each server uses, mode/VLANs and port-channel. They also become linux client containers in containerlab.
servers.renders: interface Ethernet5 / channel-group 5 mode active; interface Port-Channel5 / switchport trunk allowed vlan 11-12,21-22 / mlag 5 / spanning-tree portfast
pitfalls: switches, switch_ports and endpoint_ports are index-aligned lists of the same length.
Two switches of one MLAG pair + port_channel.mode → one MLAG port-channel (`mlag <id>`); two non-MLAG switches need an ethernet_segment (EVPN multihoming).
Endpoints only render on node types with connected_endpoints (l3leaf, l2leaf …), not on spines.

campus-fabric.learn: Teaches how eos_designs models a campus rather than a data center: the l3spine/l2leaf node types, `uplink_switches` with explicit `uplink_switch_interfaces` (so each IDF lands on the spine ports you choose), mixed MLAG and non-MLAG IDFs, a two-tier IDF (LEAF3A/B aggregating LEAF3C-E), `filter.tags` to only carry an IDF's VLANs where they are needed, `network_ports` (regex switch match + port ranges) with a `port_profiles` entry for 802.1X, phone VLANs and PoE, and `core_interfaces.p2p_links` for the routed OSPF uplinks to the WAN (the WAN router is outside the fabric and appears as a plain linux node in the lab). In the lab, IDF2's 720XP platform is replaced by cEOSLab (no PoE/dot1x hardware), so those lines are rendered only where the platform supports them. AVD doc: https://avd.arista.com/6.4/ansible_collections/arista/avd/examples/campus-fabric/index.html

custom.learn: Bring your own AVD inventory: avdlab builds it with pyavd exactly as eos_designs/eos_cli_config_gen would and turns the fabric topology CSV into a containerlab topology. Use it to lab a production design or any AVD example not in the catalogue. AVD doc: https://avd.arista.com/6.4/ansible_collections/arista/avd/roles/eos_designs/index.html

cv-pathfinder.learn: Teaches the AVD WAN data model: `wan_mode: cv-pathfinder`, the wan_rr (pathfinder) and wan_router node types, `cv_pathfinder_regions/sites` and transit modes, `wan_carriers` → `wan_path_groups` (trusted MPLS vs. untrusted Internet), WAN `l3_interfaces` with `l3_interface_profiles`, `wan_ha`, `wan_virtual_topologies` (per-VRF policies with preferred/alternate path groups, application profiles, DSCP and jitter/latency/loss constraints) and `application_classification`, plus how the LAN side attaches (`uplink_type: p2p-vrfs | lan | p2p`). The generated configs show `router path-selection`, `router adaptive-virtual-topology`, IPsec profiles and the EVPN/VXLAN overlay to the pathfinders. In containerlab (cEOS) the BGP/EVPN/IPsec control plane comes up, but the WAN data plane (DPS path selection) needs real CloudEOS/hardware and CloudVision Pathfinder. AVD doc: https://avd.arista.com/6.4/ansible_collections/arista/avd/examples/cv-pathfinder/index.html
cv-pathfinder.notes: WAN path-selection needs CloudVision Pathfinder; cEOS supports the control plane only

dual-dc-l3ls.learn: Teaches multi-site EVPN: two independent L3LS fabrics (DC1, DC2) in one inventory, each with its own spines, pools and ASNs, stitched together at the leaf pairs acting as EVPN gateways (`evpn_gateway.evpn_l2` / `evpn_gateway.evpn_l3` and `evpn_gateway.remote_peers` pointing at the gateways of the other DC). Look at the EVPN-OVERLAY-CORE peer group AVD renders for the gateway sessions, the multi-hop eBGP to the remote DC, and how the same tenants/VNIs span both DCs. AVD doc: https://avd.arista.com/6.4/ansible_collections/arista/avd/examples/dual-dc-l3ls/index.html

isis-ldp-ipvpn.learn: Teaches the MPLS side of eos_designs: the p / pe / rr node types, `underlay_routing_protocol: isis-ldp` with `isis_system_id_prefix` per node type, `core_interfaces` (p2p_links with an IP pool and a profile carrying the IS-IS metric/circuit type/MD5 authentication), `mpls_route_reflectors` building the iBGP VPN-IPv4 overlay, and `tenants` with `address_families: [vpn-ipv4]`, per-VRF `l3_interfaces` (sub-interfaces towards CEs), OSPF PE-CE and eBGP `bgp_peers`. Read the configs for `router isis`, `mpls ldp`, `router bgp` VPN-IPv4 and the VRF RD/RT that AVD derives from `vrf_id`. AVD doc: https://avd.arista.com/6.4/ansible_collections/arista/avd/examples/isis-ldp-ipvpn/index.html

l2ls-fabric.learn: Teaches the layer-2 leaf-spine design: `underlay_routing_protocol: none`, an MLAG spine pair (l3spine) acting as the default gateway for every VLAN (SVIs with `ip_virtual_router_addresses`, VARP), L2 leafs in MLAG pairs with port-channel uplinks to the spines (`uplink_switches` + `uplink_interfaces`), spanning-tree priorities per node type, and connected endpoints (firewall, hosts) on the leafs. A good first lab before EVPN/VXLAN. AVD doc: https://avd.arista.com/6.4/ansible_collections/arista/avd/examples/l2ls-fabric/index.html

single-dc-l3ls.learn: Teaches the reference AVD design end to end: node types spine / l3leaf / l2leaf, node ids and the IP math behind loopback, VTEP, P2P uplink and MLAG pools (`loopback_ipv4_offset`, `uplink_ipv4_pool`, `max_uplink_switches`), eBGP underlay with one ASN per leaf pair, eBGP EVPN overlay with the spines as route servers, MLAG pairs with the shared VTEP, tenants → VRFs (`vrf_vni`) → SVIs (`ip_address_virtual`) → L2VNIs (`mac_vrf_vni_base`), and connected endpoints with MLAG port-channels. Every count and pool is a knob, so you can change the fabric size and watch the configs, the topology and the ANTA catalogs follow. AVD doc: https://avd.arista.com/6.4/ansible_collections/arista/avd/examples/single-dc-l3ls/index.html

single-dc-l3ls-ipv6.learn: Teaches how an IPv6 underlay changes the AVD inputs: `underlay_ipv6: true` + `underlay_ipv6_numbered: true`, `loopback_ipv6_pool`, `vtep_loopback_ipv6_pool`, `uplink_ipv6_pool`, `mlag_peer_address_family: ipv6` with the MLAG IPv6 pools, `fabric_ip_addressing` prefix lengths, and `router_id_pool` (an IPv4 router-id is still required when loopbacks are IPv6-only). On the service side it shows `ipv6_address_virtuals` next to `ip_address_virtual` and `vtep_diagnostic` loopbacks. Compare the configs with single-dc-l3ls: peer groups IPv6-UNDERLAY-PEERS / MLAG-IPv6-UNDERLAY-PEER, `ipv6 unicast-routing` and VXLAN with an IPv6 source interface. AVD doc: https://avd.arista.com/6.4/ansible_collections/arista/avd/examples/single-dc-l3ls-ipv6/index.html

single-dc-multipod-l3ls.learn: Teaches the 5-stage Clos: a `super_spine` layer above per-pod spines (the spines' `uplink_switches` are the super-spines), one inventory group per pod with its own spines and leafs, leaf ASNs auto-assigned from a range (`bgp_as: 65100-65199`), and the super-spines as EVPN route servers (`evpn_role: server` on the super-spines, `evpn_route_servers` on the spines). Compare the underlay sessions spine ↔ super-spine with the overlay sessions and follow a VNI from a leaf in POD1 to a leaf in POD2. AVD doc: https://avd.arista.com/6.4/ansible_collections/arista/avd/examples/single-dc-multipod-l3ls/index.html
